title: Ardas close
hook: the history and hope of a whole people in one prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, benti: inside the inherited prayer, the reason for today is yours to say. Today we close this part of the path and see the Ardas whole.

For thirty-five days we've taken one prayer apart, line by line, the way you might take apart a watch to see how it ticks. Now put it back together. Picture it all at once: a few minutes long, said standing, every day, in every gurdwara, in kitchens and hospital rooms and airports. And inside those few minutes, a whole people's story, from its first Guru to this morning's family asking for help with a new job.
screen: `THIRTY-FIVE DAYS, ONE PRAYER.` → `PUT IT BACK TOGETHER.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE'S STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the Ardas as a map. It opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh: first remember the Divine, then Guru Nanak, and it walks name by name through the ten Gurus, ending with the Guru Granth Sahib. Then it remembers. The Panj Piare, the five beloved ones. The four Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons. The martyrs, named by what they endured, and those who served in the langar and kept faith under pressure. Then places: the five takhts, the seats of authority, and all the gurdwaras, including the ones left behind across the border. Then it asks: for the gift of Sikhi, faith, discernment, the Name; honor for the humble, strength for the weak, shelter for the shelterless. Then the petition, today's reason, in plain words. Forgiveness for any slip. And the last line: rising spirits, good for all. Look at the order: remember, then ask, then widen. A Sikh standing for the Ardas first places themselves inside a long line of Gurus, martyrs and ordinary servers. Only then do they bring their own small need, and they end by asking good for everyone. The history is the remembering; the hope is the last line. The words have grown over time. The Rehat Maryada gives the standard text, and the remembrance of martyrs reaches into the eighteenth century and beyond. That's part of the point: the Ardas is a living prayer that a people keeps adding its story to.
screen: `FIRST REMEMBER: THE TEN GURUS.` · `THE MARTYRS AND THE PLACES.` · `THEN ASK: FOR SIKHI, FOR TODAY.` · `END WIDE: GOOD FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A WHOLE PEOPLE PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Walk the map in your mind, one breath for each stop: the Gurus, the five beloved ones, the martyrs, the gurdwaras near and far, the humble and the weak, your own reason today, forgiveness for your slips, good for all. Go slowly, and let each stop be a picture, not a word. If you pray, you can close with a quiet Waheguru; if not, simply let the map rest in you.
Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons: remembered in the Ardas alongside the Panj Piare and the martyrs, before it asks for the Name and for today, and ends with good for all.
Your line: a whole people prays. Tomorrow the path turns to hymns for every part of a life. Thirty-five days, one prayer, whole.

howItsDone: Sikhs say the full Ardas standing at the close of services and many daily prayers: it remembers the Gurus, the martyrs and the gurdwaras, makes the day's petition, and ends with good for all.
